extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political science, journalism, and media studies; informed general readers interested in public opinion and news
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and practical criteria for how public opinion is formed and how news/propaganda shape the 'pseudo-environment' that guides political behavior. Focuses on censorship, channels of communication, press behavior, and limits on access to facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-environment determines behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Each man's actions are based not on direct and certain knowledge, but on 'pictures made by himself or given to him' — 'The way in which the world is imagined determines at any particular moment what men will do.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: if someone's atlas says the world is flat he avoids sailing near the edge; if maps promise a fountain of youth an explorer will search for it. Propaganda works by altering these pictures (e.g., Marxian communists forming class-conscious groups). The pseudo-environment determines effort, feelings, and hopes, not necessarily actual accomplishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors limiting access to the facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Chief factors which limit people's access to the real environment: artificial censorships, limitations of social contact, meager time available for attention to public affairs, compression of events into very short messages, difficulty of small vocabulary expressing a complicated world, and fear of facing threatening facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this list to evaluate how incomplete or distorted the public's information is. These external limits precede and condition how messages are received and interpreted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stored images and preconceptions shape reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Messages from outside are affected by stored-up images, preconceptions, and prejudices which fill them out and in turn direct attention and vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how stereotypes and prior beliefs identify incoming information with an individual's perceived interests; study how limited messages form patterns of stereotypes that become the basis for opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression and vocabulary constraints distort news
rubrics_metrics.description: Events must often be compressed into very short messages and expressed with a small vocabulary, which introduces distortion and simplification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating news or public opinion, note where compression truncates nuance and where limited terms force complex situations into inadequate categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship and privacy create the barrier enabling propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Without some form of censorship (or limiting of access) propaganda in the strict sense is impossible: 'there must be some barrier between the public and the event.' Privacy norms and accepted secrecy functions similarly as barriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military censorship is the simplest explicit form; but legal, social, and customary privacy practices (e.g., privileged conversations, directors' meetings, cabinet secrecy) also limit access and make managed representations possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of correspondents and selection shapes public perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities (e.g., a General Staff) can control selection of correspondents, their movements, their reports, and the wires — thereby shaping what the public will perceive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use wartime communique examples: the French General Staff chose which correspondents went to the front, censored their messages, and operated the wires to present a chosen picture (e.g., framing Verdun as attrition in the Allies' favor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing and repetition produce inferences without argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated formulae or emphasized data (like casualty figures) create a mental picture and lead the public to particular inferences without formal argumentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: French communiques repeatedly highlighted German losses and omitted French casualties to create belief in a favorable attrition strategy. Repetition and selective framing can neutralize contrary impressions and produce acquiescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy norms and conventions are variable barriers to knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Notions of privacy—what is 'public' versus 'private'—change over time and across topics; many matters are treated as none of the public's business and thereby excluded from public knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how conventions (income privacy, corporate secrecy, privileged communications) restrict who has access to facts; ask how you got the facts behind an opinion, who actually observed them, and how much they were permitted to see.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact and opportunity constraints on circulation of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: There are strong limits upon the circulation of ideas: reaching 'everybody' requires massive, organized efforts (e.g., wartime propaganda campaigns); in peace time many groups remain in enclaves and hear little of larger affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reach by examining channels used (speeches, printed releases, posters, schools, civic organizations) and note that in normal conditions such comprehensive penetration is rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical, economic, and political infrastructure affects information flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Means of communication and transport (railways, cables, ports, tariffs, monopolies, customs, costs) influence the supply and quality of information and create barriers to exchange of news and opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: monopolizing cables or ports or prohibitive costs of travel isolate populations; changes in transport or cables can open or close channels of opinion circulation—these are structural determinants to evaluate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socioeconomic status affects access to the world beyond one's neighborhood
rubrics_metrics.description: A person's income and position affect his access to information about wider affairs; lower incomes or insular occupations limit exposure to broader news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing public opinion, factor in who hears what: ghettoes, enclaves, and classes may be largely uninformed of matters outside their immediate concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between psychoanalytic and social-analytic criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychoanalysts study individual's maladjustment to an environment assumed to be knowable; the social analyst studies how the larger political environment is conceived—the pseudo-environment—and must not assume a 'normal' social career as a neutral standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using clinical/individual 'normality' as a criterion for social judgments about public opinion. The sociologist should examine how images and preconceptions are formed socially rather than assuming an objectively knowable environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative government requires independent expert interpretation of unseen facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative government cannot function successfully unless augmented by independent expert organizations that make 'the unseen facts intelligible' to decision-makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The press cannot be relied upon to perform this function at no cost; political science or expert bodies should organize public opinions for the press in advance of decisions rather than leaving the press to apologize or simply report after decisions are made.
